Extending RdistNN: custom distances, rank weights, and scores

Source: vignettes/extending.Rmd
extending.Rmd

Choose an extension point

Most extensions replace one part of the estimation pipeline:

Goal Extension
Change closeness or observation ordering Distance or ranking provider
Change the weight profile for given ranks Rank-weight rule
Change the order s for a given (n, kx, k) Tuning specification
Evaluate another kernel on data subsets Score
Reuse external distances, orders or ranks weights_matrix(ranking = ...)

Use as_distance(), as_rank_weight() or as_score() for a simple function. Their new_*() counterparts support batch evaluation, setup context and parameter-aware score derivatives.

For kernel-order specifications, use Kernel-order tuning. For result classes and reporting conventions, use Notation and conventions.

Custom distances

Quick Prototype With as_distance()

Use as_distance() when a simple function (X, x0, ctx) -> numeric(n) is enough.

# L-infinity distance
linf <- as_distance(
  function(X, x0, ctx = NULL) {
    apply(abs(X - matrix(x0, nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE)), 1L, max)
  },
  name = "linf"
)

register_distance("linf", linf)
distance_names()
#> [1] "l1"           "l1_scaled_sd" "l2"           "l2_scaled_sd" "l2_sq"       
#> [6] "linf"         "mahalanobis"

You can test the distance directly before registering it:

X <- matrix(rnorm(40), 20, 2)
x0 <- c(0, 0)

distance_eval(linf, X, x0)
#>  [1] 0.9619334 0.9423007 0.2587882 1.6664748 0.4844551 0.7410727 1.1606158
#>  [8] 1.1166102 1.2188574 1.2673687 0.9006247 1.1312186 0.7277152 0.7365021
#> [15] 0.3521296 0.7055155 1.3003580 0.6482428 1.2243136 0.7937612
dim(distance_eval_batch(linf, X[1L, , drop = FALSE], rbind(x0, x0)))
#> [1] 1 2

Reusable Distance With new_distance(), setup(), and eval_batch()

Use new_distance() when you want to precompute context once on X and reuse it across many targets.

scaled_l2 <- new_distance(
  name = "scaled_l2_demo",
  setup = function(X) {
    scale <- apply(X, 2L, stats::sd)
    scale[!is.finite(scale) | scale <= 0] <- 1
    list(scale = scale)
  },
  eval_batch = function(X, X0, ctx) {
    D <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X0)), function(j) {
      delta <- sweep(X, 2L, X0[j, ], "-")
      sqrt(rowSums(sweep(delta, 2L, ctx$scale, "/")^2))
    }, numeric(nrow(X)))
    matrix(D, nrow = nrow(X), ncol = nrow(X0))
  }
)

X <- matrix(rnorm(80), 40, 2)
X0 <- matrix(rnorm(12), 6, 2)

ctx_dist <- scaled_l2$setup(X)
D <- distance_eval_batch(scaled_l2, X, X0, ctx = ctx_dist)
dim(D)
#> [1] 40  6

Batch distances have shape n x m, including a single observation or target. A custom eval_batch() must return an actual matrix with those dimensions. Scalar-only specs use the shared batch evaluator, which assembles the matrix without dropping singleton dimensions. With ctx = NULL, distance-side setup(X) runs once per batch, including calls through weights_matrix(). Pass a fitted context explicitly to reuse it across calls.

Custom rank weights

Rank weights only see integer ranks, not raw distances. Rank 1 means “closest observation,” rank 2 means “second closest,” and so on.

That separation is useful because you can change the localization profile without changing the ranking logic.

Quick Prototype With as_rank_weight() 

rw_inv <- as_rank_weight(
  function(ranks, ctx = NULL) {
    w <- 1 / as.numeric(ranks)
    w / sum(w)
  },
  name = "inv_rank"
)

register_rank_weight("inv_rank", rw_inv)
rank_weight_names()
#> [1] "inv_rank"
dim(rank_weight_eval_batch(rw_inv, matrix(1L, nrow = 1L, ncol = 2L)))
#> [1] 1 2

A Compact-Support Rule

This example keeps only the first m closest observations in rank order. That is a generic finite-support rule. It is not the same thing as exact DNN.

make_top_m <- function(m) {
  if (length(m) != 1L || !is.numeric(m) || !is.finite(m) || m < 1 || m != floor(m)) {
    stop("`m` must be a positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  as_rank_weight(
    function(ranks) {
      keep <- as.numeric(ranks <= m)
      keep / sum(keep)
    },
    name = paste0("top_", m)
  )
}

rw_top10 <- make_top_m(10L)

rank_weight_eval() evaluates the supplied rank rule without covariate groups. When that rule is passed to weights_matrix(), the covariate-aware layer averages its assigned weights within exactly identical raw-X groups, including signed or unnormalized rules. A support boundary inside a group can therefore give nonzero observation weights beyond the original cutoff. Custom rankers remain responsible for their own ordering policy. See DNN weights and ranks for the grouping rule, deletion redistribution and theory warning.

Batched Rank Weights and Shared ctx

For performance, prefer eval_batch() once the prototype is stable. Scalar-only rules are evaluated and validated one target at a time; their batch output stays n x m even when either dimension is one. A custom batch callback must itself return an n x m matrix.

rw_exp <- new_rank_weight(
  name = "exp_decay",
  eval_batch = function(R, ctx = NULL) {
    lambda <- if (is.null(ctx) || is.null(ctx$lambda)) 0.25 else ctx$lambda
    W <- exp(-lambda * (R - 1L))
    sweep(W, 2L, colSums(W), "/")
  }
)

R <- cbind(1:5, c(2L, 1L, 3L, 4L, 5L))
rank_weight_eval_batch(rw_exp, R, ctx = list(lambda = 0.5))
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 0.42865553 0.25999272
#> [2,] 0.25999272 0.42865553
#> [3,] 0.15769356 0.15769356
#> [4,] 0.09564598 0.09564598
#> [5,] 0.05801222 0.05801222

At the top level, weights_matrix() passes any supplied ctx through to both the ranking and weight evaluators. If both sides need context, build one shared list.

weights_matrix() does not call rank-weight-side setup() automatically. Close over fixed parameters in the constructor, or build and pass a shared ctx when both the ranking and weights need context.

Combine ranking and weights

weights_matrix() is the main modular entry point. The ranking argument can be:

  • a distance spec or registered distance name;
  • a function (X, X0, ctx) that returns dx, ord, or ranks;
  • a precomputed list with dx, ord, or ranks;
  • a ranks matrix directly.

That makes it the right place to integrate custom ranking code, precomputed distances, or external nearest-neighbor engines.

n <- 80
p <- 2
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
X0 <- matrix(rnorm(4 * p), 4, p)

# If only the distance needs setup, leave ctx = NULL and let the distance
# auto-setup path run.
out1 <- weights_matrix(
  X = X,
  X0 = X0,
  ranking = scaled_l2,
  weight = rw_top10,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ord", "ranks")
)

# If both the distance and the weight need context, build one shared list.
ctx_both <- c(scaled_l2$setup(X), list(lambda = 0.35))
out2 <- weights_matrix(
  X = X,
  X0 = X0,
  ranking = scaled_l2,
  weight = rw_exp,
  ctx = ctx_both,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ord", "ranks")
)

dim(out2$W)
#> [1] 80  4

For debugging custom ranking behavior, request the intermediate objects:

lapply(out2[c("dx", "ord", "ranks", "W")], function(x) head(x[, 1L]))
#> $dx
#> [1] 2.2488708 0.7809354 1.4038669 1.4214305 1.9483745 2.3285028
#> 
#> $ord
#> [1] 80 29 42 60 68 16
#> 
#> $ranks
#> [1] 64 16 42 44 57 67
#> 
#> $W
#> [1] 7.835877e-11 1.549655e-03 1.730434e-07 8.593083e-08 9.080487e-10
#> [6] 2.742069e-11

Custom scores

The score layer is separate from localization. A score describes what happens once a subset of observations has been selected.

Quick Prototype With as_score()

Use as_score() for a simple kernel with fixed order s. Each scalar callback must return one finite numeric value per subset. Logical values and multiple values are rejected before the batch output is assembled.

sc_avg2 <- as_score(
  function(idxs, data, ctx = NULL, rng = NULL) {
    mean(data$Y[idxs])
  },
  s = 2L,
  name = "avg2"
)

register_score("avg2", sc_avg2)
list_scores()
#> [1] "avg2"

df <- data.frame(Y = rnorm(10))
subs <- rbind(c(1L, 2L), c(4L, 8L), c(3L, 9L))
score_eval_batch(sc_avg2, subs = subs, data = df)
#> [1] -0.2481958 -0.0925133 -0.3545440

Reusable Score With new_score() and setup()

Use setup() when the score repeatedly accesses the same data columns or transformed objects.

sc_pair_gap <- new_score(
  name = "pair_gap_sq",
  order = 2L,
  setup = function(data, ...) list(y = as.numeric(data$Y)),
  eval_batch = function(subs, data, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    (ctx$y[subs[, 1L]] - ctx$y[subs[, 2L]])^2
  }
)

df <- data.frame(Y = rnorm(10))
ctx_score <- score_setup(sc_pair_gap, df)
subs <- rbind(c(1L, 2L), c(2L, 5L), c(3L, 4L))

score_eval_batch(sc_pair_gap, subs, data = df, ctx = ctx_score)
#> [1] 0.1578244 2.4352638 9.0069443

Parameter-Aware Scores And Derivatives With score_diff_path()

If your score depends on a parameter vector, implement eval_param or an eval that accepts theta, then use score_diff_path() to get reusable value and gradient closures. An analytic batch gradient must be a two-dimensional K x p matrix for K subsets and p parameters. When p = 1, a numeric vector of length K is also accepted and converted to that matrix; higher-dimensional arrays are rejected.

sc_affine <- new_score(
  name = "affine_order1",
  order = 1L,
  eval_param = function(idxs, data, theta, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    theta[1] * data$Y[idxs] + theta[2]
  },
  grad = function(idxs, data, theta, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    c(data$Y[idxs], 1)
  }
)

df <- data.frame(Y = c(1, 2, 4))
path <- score_diff_path(sc_affine, data = df, method = "auto")

path$value(2L, theta = c(0.5, 1))
#> [1] 2
path$grad(2L, theta = c(0.5, 1))
#> [1] 2 1

score_diff_path() evaluates its data argument when the path is created. Rebinding df later does not change the data used by this path. Custom closures, environments and external pointers can still contain mutable state; their authors remain responsible for reproducible evaluations.

If you do not provide an analytic gradient, score_diff_path(..., method = "fd") uses finite differences based on eval_param / eval_param_batch.

A minimal estimator

The modular API is meant to let you assemble your own localized estimators without rewriting the whole package. A minimal pattern is:

my_local_mean <- function(X, x0, y, ranking = "l2", weight) {
  W <- weights_matrix(
    X = X,
    x0 = x0,
    ranking = ranking,
    weight = weight,
    return = "W"
  )$W[, 1L]

  sum(W * y)
}

my_local_mean(X, x0 = X0[1, ], y = X[, 1], weight = rw_top10)
#> [1] -0.7872897

For more complicated estimators, replace the scalar y contribution with your own score or estimating equation.

Check an extension

Test the evaluator on a small dataset before registering its name. Check its output shape and finite values, and request W, dx, ord and ranks to inspect the weighting pipeline. Specs receive ranks rather than raw distances; when both ranking and weighting need setup, pass an explicit shared ctx.

Custom estimators need their own statistical justification. The examples here show software composition; the paper and its references give the background for the package’s estimators.
